reading.body:
S. 1792, the AI Whistleblower Protection Act, has drawn 23 lobbying filings and 14 cosponsors, with the largest share of filings coming from Meta and two BSA entities.

The cosponsor list is bipartisan and unusually broad, running from Grassley and Blackburn on the Republican side to Schumer, Durbin, and Blumenthal on the Democratic side. That spread suggests the bill's subject, protections for people who report on AI systems, is not currently a partisan dividing line in the way that many AI governance proposals are.

The lobbying record points the other way. Meta accounts for 6 filings, the two BSA entries for 9 between them, and Google for 4, so the bulk of the named activity comes from large platform and software trade interests rather than from civil society. Transparency International and the AI Policy Network appear with 2 and 1 filings. A filing that names a bill shows the bill was an issue in the lobbying, not the position taken on it, so this data establishes who is watching the bill, not who opposes it.

The bill's own text is tagged to jobs and workforce and to bias and civil rights, which places it in the labor and civil rights side of AI policy rather than in the compute, data center, or power side. Nothing here speaks to how AI systems are built or where they run. The record also stops at a status date of 2025-05-15 and does not show committee action, amendments, or a floor vote, so it cannot tell the reader whether the bill is advancing or stalled.

summary: S. 1792, AI Whistleblower Protection Act. Latest status date 2025-05-15. Issues tagged from the bill's own text: jobs and workforce, bias and civil rights. 23 lobbying filing(s) for 2025 or later name it.
